newsitem.title: INDIA: India must focus on infrastructure - Ahluwalia.
newsitem.headline: India must focus on infrastructure - Ahluwalia.

text.p: India must focus on overhauling the infrastructure sector in the next phase of economic reforms to achieve higher growth, Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia was quoted on Wednesday as saying.
" I think we have a lot to do in the infrastructure sector," Ahluwalia, the highest ranking civil servant in the Finance Ministry, told the Business Standard newspaper in an interview.
India began liberalising its economy in 1991 under former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, opening up trade and industry and dismantling decades old socialist controls.
The government needs to strengthen state-owned firms operating in core infrastructure sectors, including restructuring their finances, said Ahluwalia.
"State electricity boards are in a complete mess because of unviable tariffs and this cannot continue."
Ahluwalia hoped for a better performance by state electricity boards in 1996/97 (April-March).

"One of ways in which the system has responded to the infrastructure constraints of the state electricity boards is there is a lot of private generating capacity," he said, noting private power generating capacity stood at 10,000 megawatts.
There was also a need to speed up private investment in infrastructure, he added.
"Private sector investors need an environment of financial viability and very strong risk mitigation which involves a very complex legal structure," Ahluwalia said.
India has gained considerable experience in privatisation, particularly in the telecommunications industry, and untied complex knots, he added. "So I think we need to concentrate on that."
Ahluwalia reiterated the government's view that India can achieve gross domestic product (GDP) growth of seven percent in 1997/98 and hold the inflation rate below seven percent.
"From the macro point of view, if we get 7.0 percent GDP growth, then 16 percent M-3 growth is quite consistent with bringing the inflation below seven percent," he said.
M-3 measures the growth in aggregate money supply in the economy.
The government estimates real GDP is expected to grow by 6.8 percent in 1996/97 compared with 7.1 percent growth in 1995/96.
Ahluwalia said industrial production is expected to grow by 10 percent in the next fiscal year beginning on April 1.

"We could easily have 10 percent growth in industry. If in agriculture you get a growth rate of 3.5 percent and services grow at about 8.0 percent, it will add up to 7.0 percent in GDP growth," he said.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, in the 1997/98 federal budget presented last week, slashed corporate taxes and import tariffs, and proposed a string of incentives to capital markets to boost economic growth.
"The whole thrust of continuing tax reform gives a very big signal on the investment front," Ahluwalia said.
He said the tax reforms along with the objective of reducing the fiscal deficit to 4.5 percent of GDP in 1997/98 from an estimated 5.0 percent in 1996/97 will put less pressure on interest rates.

"We are also trying to improve the market for government debt," said Ahluwalia. The government has taken several steps in the last few months to spur the debt market, including allowing foreign institutional investors (FIIs) to invest in government securities, he added.
"All these developments point to lower interest rates and improved flow of savings into the capital markets," Ahluwalia said.
He expected foreign investment inflow to grow in 1997/98 and said a slowdown in export growth was unlikely to exert pressure on the balance of payments.
